units.text: INT. FAN - CONTINUOUS
FOURTH ACT
Lying on sofa .

How can I tell him? I can’t tell him. It would kill me. I wonder what happened after I escaped from that horrible room. Perhaps she told them the true reason of her being there, and the real meaning of that—fatal fan of mine. Oh, if he knows—how can I look him in the face again? He would never forgive me.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Touches bell .
How securely one thinks one lives—out of reach of temptation, sin, folly. And then suddenly—Oh! Life is terrible. It rules us, we do not rule it.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Enter ROSALIE R.
Did your ladyship ring for me?
units.name: ROSALIE

units.text: Yes. Have you found out at what time Lord Windermere came in last night?
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: His lordship did not come in till five o’clock.
units.name: ROSALIE

units.text: Five o’clock? He knocked at my door this morning, didn’t he?
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Yes, my lady—at half-past nine. I told him your ladyship was not awake yet.
units.name: ROSALIE

units.text: Did he say anything?
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Something about your ladyship’s fan. I didn’t quite catch what his lordship said. Has the fan been lost, my lady? I can’t find it, and Parker says it was not left in any of the rooms. He has looked in all of them and on the terrace as well.
units.name: ROSALIE

units.text: It doesn’t matter. Tell Parker not to trouble. That will do.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Exit ROSALIE.
Rising .

She is sure to tell him. I can fancy a person doing a wonderful act of self-sacrifice, doing it spontaneously, recklessly, nobly—and afterwards finding out that it costs too much. Why should she hesitate between her ruin and mine? . . . How strange! I would have publicly disgraced her in my own house. She accepts public disgrace in the house of another to save me. . . . There is a bitter irony in things, a bitter irony in the way we talk of good and bad women. . . . Oh, what a lesson! and what a pity that in life we only get our lessons when they are of no use to us! For even if she doesn’t tell, I must. Oh! the shame of it, the shame of it. To tell it is to live through it all again. Actions are the first tragedy in life, words are the second. Words are perhaps the worst. Words are merciless. . . . Oh!
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Starts as LORD WINDERMERE enters .
Kisses her .
Margaret—how pale you look!
units.name: LORD WINDERMERE

units.text: I slept very badly.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Sitting on sofa with her .
I am so sorry. I came in dreadfully late, and didn’t like to wake you. You are crying, dear.
units.name: LORD WINDERMERE

units.text: Yes, I am crying, for I have something to tell you, Arthur.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: My dear child, you are not well. You’ve been doing too much. Let us go away to the country. You’ll be all right at Selby. The season is almost over. There is no use staying on. Poor darling! We’ll go away to-day, if you like.
units.name: LORD WINDERMERE

units.text: Rises .
We can easily catch the 3.40. I’ll send a wire to Fannen.
units.name: LORD WINDERMERE

units.text: Crosses and sits down at table to write a telegram .
Yes; let us go away to-day. No; I can’t go to-day, Arthur. There is some one I must see before I leave town—some one who has been kind to me.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Rising and leaning over sofa .
Kind to you?
units.name: LORD WINDERMERE

units.text: Far more than that.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Rises and goes to him .
I will tell you, Arthur, but only love me, love me as you used to love me.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: Used to? You are not thinking of that wretched woman who came here last night?
units.name: LORD WINDERMERE

units.text: Coming round and sitting R. of her .
You don’t still imagine—no, you couldn’t.
units.name: LORD WINDERMERE

units.text: I don’t. I know now I was wrong and foolish.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: It was very good of you to receive her last night—but you are never to see her again.
units.name: LORD WINDERMERE

units.text: Why do you say that?
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: A pause .
Holding her hand .

Margaret, I thought Mrs. Erlynne was a woman more sinned against than sinning, as the phrase goes. I thought she wanted to be good, to get back into a place that she had lost by a moment’s folly, to lead again a decent life. I believed what she told me—I was mistaken in her. She is bad—as bad as a woman can be.
units.name: LORD WINDERMERE

units.text: Arthur, Arthur, don’t talk so bitterly about any woman. I don’t think now that people can be divided into the good and the bad as though they were two separate races or creations. What are called good women may have terrible things in them, mad moods of recklessness, assertion, jealousy, sin. Bad women, as they are termed, may have in them sorrow, repentance, pity, sacrifice. And I don’t think Mrs. Erlynne a bad woman—I know she’s not.
units.name: LADY WINDERMERE

units.text: My dear child, the woman’s impossible. No matter what harm she tries to do us, you must never see her again. She is inadmissible anywhere.
units.name: LORD WINDERMERE
